title: Surgery equipment: chair, suction & curing light
blurb: The dental chair, high- and low-volume suction, the curing light, amalgamator and compressor: how to use them, check them and keep them working.
question: During a posterior composite, the dentist cures each layer holding the light tip well above the tooth, and you notice the tip is crusted with old resin. At the end of the session the suction is gurgling and weak. What risks do you need to raise, and what checks and maintenance should you be doing?

teach.h: Equipment you set up, check and maintain
teach.body: The dental nurse looks after the surgery's equipment day to day: the chair and delivery unit, the operating light, suction, curing light, amalgamator and the compressor that drives the air-powered kit. Equipment that isn't checked, cleaned and serviced can fail mid-treatment, spread infection or harm the patient. So practices keep recorded maintenance: daily checks, servicing and statutory inspections, all logged. Spotting and reporting a fault is part of your responsibility for the quality and safety of the care the patient receives.

teach.h: Working zones round the chair (right-handed dentist)
teach.caption: Clock positions with the patient's head at 12. Textbooks vary slightly on the exact ranges; this is a common convention. Instruments are passed in the transfer zone, over the chest, never over the face. The zones are mirrored for a left-handed dentist.

teach.body: Most treatment is done with the patient lying back (supine). Impressions are often taken upright, and patients with breathing difficulties may need to sit up. If a patient feels faint, lay the chair flat and raise the legs. Check the chair's upholstery is intact, because torn covers can't be cleaned, and clean touch points between patients. Angle the operating light into the mouth, not the eyes, and offer the patient protective glasses.

values: Keep the floor of mouth dry

teach.caption: A narrow surgical aspirator tip is used for oral surgery, and portable suction is kept for medical emergencies.

teach.h: Suction care at the end of the session

steps.label: Flush
steps.sub: Draw a non-foaming suction cleaner through every hose

steps.label: Clean the filter
steps.sub: Remove and clean or replace the trap

steps.label: Amalgam waste
steps.sub: Trap contents in the white amalgam container

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: Log it on the maintenance sheet

teach.caption: Weak or gurgling suction often means a blocked filter or hose. An amalgam separator in the system stops amalgam particles reaching the drains.

head: Part
Check
rows: Set to the material's cure time
teach.caption: The curing light gives out intense blue light. The orange shield or orange glasses filter it to protect the eyes of everyone watching.

teach.body: Light-cured composite, sealants, liners and bonding agents contain a photoinitiator that starts setting (polymerising) when blue light hits it. Modern LED lights produce that blue light. The light is intense enough to damage the retina, so the orange shield or orange glasses filter it out for everyone watching. Light output falls quickly with distance, and resin stuck on the tip blocks it. Either way, the material under-cures and the restoration can fail.

items: Check it is charged and the tip is clean, undamaged and covered with a barrier sleeve.
Position the orange shield, or give the team and patient orange glasses.
Hold the tip as close to the material as possible without touching it, square on to the surface.
Cure for the time the material's manufacturer states, one increment at a time.
Check the light's output regularly with a radiometer (light meter) and record it.

head: Equipment
What it does
Key check
teach.caption: Compressors are pressure systems covered by the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000, so they are examined by a competent person as the practice's written scheme sets out.

teach.text: Holding the curing light further away does NOT make it 'cure a wider area'. Light intensity drops sharply with distance, so the composite under-cures. Close, square on, clean tip, full time.

items: High-volume aspiration removes spray, debris and aerosol; the saliva ejector removes pooling saliva.
Clean suction lines with a non-foaming cleaner and clean the filter at the end of each session; trap contents go in amalgam waste.
Curing light: orange shield, tip close and clean, manufacturer's time, regular radiometer checks.
If equipment is faulty: stop using it, label it, report it, record it and arrange repair. Adverse incidents with medical devices can be reported to the MHRA (Yellow Card).
Maintenance and testing must be recorded: daily checks, servicing and statutory inspections.

summary: You can now position the patient and the team around the chair, tell high-volume from low-volume suction, clean and maintain the suction system, use a curing light safely and effectively, and explain how the amalgamator, compressor and other equipment are checked and their maintenance recorded.

A.q: Why is the orange shield positioned when the curing light is in use?
options: It speeds up the setting of the composite resin
It filters the intense blue light to protect eyes
It stops heat from the light reaching the pulp
It focuses the light beam onto the restoration surface
A.why: The orange filter blocks the intense blue light, which can damage the retina, protecting the eyes of the team and patient.

whyNot.0: The shield doesn't affect setting; the light reaching the material does.
whyNot.2: The shield sits away from the tooth and doesn't affect tooth temperature.
whyNot.3: The shield filters stray light; it doesn't focus the beam.

A.q: During a composite, the curing light is held well away from the restoration. What is the most likely result?
options: The composite cures faster
The shade becomes lighter
The composite under-cures
The tooth becomes desensitised
A.why: Light intensity falls sharply with distance, so less energy reaches the material and it may not fully set.

whyNot.0: Distance reduces the light reaching the composite, so it cures less, not faster.
whyNot.1: Shade depends on the material chosen, not curing distance.
whyNot.3: Curing distance has no desensitising effect.

A.q: What is the main role of the high-volume aspirator during cutting with the air turbine?
options: To remove water spray, debris and aerosol
To keep the patient's lips moist and comfortable
To cool the bur while the dentist is cutting
To dry the cavity ready for the bonding agent
A.why: The wide-bore high-volume aspirator removes water, debris and aerosol at source and can retract the cheek or tongue.

whyNot.1: Suction removes moisture; it doesn't keep lips moist.
whyNot.2: Cooling comes from the handpiece's water spray.
whyNot.3: The 3-in-1 air syringe dries the cavity.

B.q: The curing light tip is coated with old composite. What is the main risk if it is used without cleaning?
options: The light will overheat and switch itself off
Reduced light output reaching the material
The composite shade will change colour
The patient may feel an electric shock
B.why: Resin on the tip blocks and scatters the light, so less reaches the restoration and it may under-cure.

whyNot.0: Debris on the tip reduces output; it doesn't usually cause overheating cut-outs.
whyNot.2: Shade depends on the material chosen.
whyNot.3: The tip is a light guide and doesn't carry current to the patient.

B.q: At the end of a clinical session, how should the suction system be cleaned?
options: Draw suction cleaner through and clean the filter
Flush each hose with plenty of hot tap water only
Pour household bleach down the spittoon drain
Leave the lines alone until the annual service
B.why: A non-foaming cleaner drawn through every hose, plus cleaning the filter, keeps the lines clear and hygienic as the manufacturer recommends.

whyNot.1: Water alone doesn't disinfect the lines or break down debris.
whyNot.2: Household bleach can damage the system and isn't the manufacturer's cleaner.
whyNot.3: Suction needs cleaning every session, not just at service.

B.q: The dental chair's foot control keeps cutting out partway through a clinical session. What should you do?
options: Keep using it and mention it at the next team meeting
Try to repair the wiring yourself
Take it out of use, label it and report it
Switch it off and on and carry on if it works
B.why: Faulty equipment is taken out of use, clearly labelled, reported to the person responsible and recorded, then repaired by a competent engineer.

whyNot.0: Continuing to use faulty equipment puts patients and staff at risk.
whyNot.1: Repairs must be done by a competent engineer, not by the nurse.
whyNot.3: An intermittent fault is still a fault and must be reported.

C.q: Which piece of equipment supplies the air that drives the air turbine and 3-in-1 syringe?
options: Amalgamator
Suction motor
Compressor
Curing light
C.why: The compressor supplies compressed air to the dental unit for the turbine, 3-in-1 syringe and other air-driven equipment.

whyNot.0: The amalgamator mixes capsules by vibration.
whyNot.1: The suction motor creates negative pressure to remove fluids, the opposite job.
whyNot.3: The curing light produces blue light to set resins.

C.q: A patient says they feel faint while sitting upright in the chair. What is the best immediate chair position?
options: Sit them further upright
Lay them flat and raise the legs
Tilt their head forward
Stand them up and walk them around
C.why: Laying the patient flat with legs raised helps blood return to the brain and usually brings rapid recovery from a faint.

whyNot.0: Sitting more upright reduces blood flow to the brain and makes fainting more likely.
whyNot.2: Head forward doesn't restore blood flow to the brain.
whyNot.3: Standing a faint patient risks a fall and injury.

C.q: Which statement about a saliva ejector is correct?
options: It is wide-bore and held by the nurse
It removes aerosol from the air turbine
It is used to retract the cheek firmly
It is narrow and can rest in the mouth
C.why: The saliva ejector is a narrow, low-volume tube that can rest in the floor of the mouth to remove pooling saliva.

whyNot.1: Aerosol is captured with the high-volume aspirator close to the tooth.
whyNot.2: Firm retraction is done with the high-volume aspirator tip or a mirror.

reteach.title: Think of a torch and a vacuum cleaner
reteach.question: What happens to a torch beam as you move it away from a wall, and what happens to a vacuum cleaner with a full bag?

blocks.body: Shine a torch at a wall from close up and you get a small, bright spot. Step back and the spot spreads out and gets dimmer. A curing light does the same, so held far away it doesn't deliver enough light to set the composite. A dirty lens dims it too. A vacuum cleaner with a full bag or blocked filter loses its pull. Dental suction is the same: if the filter isn't cleaned and the lines aren't flushed every session, it gurgles and loses power.

explain.body: An LED curing light produces blue light that sets light-cured composite, sealants, liners and bonding agents. Use the orange shield, hold the tip close and square on, keep it clean and sleeved, cure for the stated time and check output with a radiometer.

test.q: Which instrument is used to check that a curing light is still giving out enough light?
options: Thermometer
Apex locator
Pressure gauge
Radiometer
test.why: A radiometer (light meter) measures the curing light's output so a failing light can be spotted.

whyNot.0: A thermometer measures temperature, not light output.
whyNot.1: An apex locator measures root canal working length.
whyNot.2: A pressure gauge is used on systems like the compressor.

explain.body: The high-volume aspirator is wide-bore and held by the nurse to remove spray, debris and aerosol. The saliva ejector is narrow and low-volume. At the end of each session, draw a non-foaming suction cleaner through and clean the filter, wearing PPE. Amalgam from the trap goes in the white amalgam waste container.

items.label: White container
items.sub: Amalgam waste, with mercury vapour suppressant

test.q: Where should the contents of the suction filter trap be disposed of?
options: Household black-bag waste
Amalgam waste container
Down the spittoon
Orange-bag clinical waste
test.why: The trap usually contains amalgam particles, which are hazardous waste and go in the marked amalgam container with mercury suppressant.

whyNot.0: Amalgam is hazardous and must never go in domestic waste.
whyNot.2: Flushing it would send mercury into the drains.
whyNot.3: Orange bags are for infectious waste treated by alternative methods, not amalgam.

explain.body: The compressor supplies clean, dry air to the turbines, 3-in-1 and chair. Moisture is drained as the manufacturer directs, and as a pressure system it is examined by a competent person. The amalgamator mixes sealed capsules by vibration, with the lid closed.

test.q: Why must the lid of the amalgamator be closed before it runs?
options: To contain the capsule if it flies out or leaks
To keep the amalgam warm while it is mixing
To stop the surgery light setting the amalgam
To measure the mixing time more accurately
test.why: The capsule vibrates at high speed; the lid contains it and any mercury vapour or fragments if it breaks open.

whyNot.1: Amalgam isn't warmed by the lid.
whyNot.2: Amalgam sets chemically, not with light.
whyNot.3: The timer controls the mixing time, not the lid.
